title: A boy's lunch (John 6:1–14)
hook: five loaves and two fish from a child, and five thousand eat with baskets left over

segments.voice: Yesterday, the woman at the well, and a long talk at noon about living water. Did you have an unhurried conversation? Today, a hillside, and a hungry crowd. Day fifty-four.

You know that moment when you look at what you've got and it's obviously not enough. Not enough money for the month. Not enough time for everything. Not enough patience for the kids tonight. Now picture a grassy hillside by the Sea of Galilee. A huge crowd has followed Jesus out there, because they've seen him heal the sick. It's getting late. There's no town nearby, no market, nothing. Jesus looks at the crowd, then turns to one of his disciples, Philip, and asks a question John says was a test: where are we going to buy bread for all these people? Today, a boy's lunch.
screen: `OBVIOUSLY NOT ENOUGH.` → `A HUNGRY CROWD ON A HILLSIDE.` → `WHERE SHALL WE BUY BREAD?`

segments.voice: Philip does the math, in the King James Bible: "Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little." A penny there is a denarius, a day's wage. So: more than half a year's pay wouldn't give everyone even a bite. Then Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, comes back with something almost funny: "There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?" Only John mentions the boy. Barley was the cheap grain, the bread of poor families. This is a kid's packed lunch. And somebody has to hand it over. Jesus has the people sit down on the grass, about five thousand men, John says, and he takes the loaves, gives thanks, and hands them out, and the fish too, as much as anyone wants. Then comes a line people skip past: "Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost." They fill twelve baskets with leftovers. Twelve, from five loaves. Nothing wasted. This is the only miracle, apart from the resurrection, that all four Gospels tell. Christians have always read it as a real wonder, and many also hear in it the table of communion, since he takes bread, gives thanks, and gives it. Later in the same chapter he calls himself the bread of life. But start with the boy. Nobody asks him to fix the problem. He just offers what he has, and it's small, and it's given away, and it turns out to be enough, with baskets to spare.
screen: `HALF A YEAR'S WAGES ISN'T ENOUGH.` · `FIVE BARLEY LOAVES, TWO FISH.` · `HE GIVES THANKS AND GIVES.` · `TWELVE BASKETS LEFT OVER.` · then, large: `THAT NOTHING BE LOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe slowly. Think of a need you know about right now. A friend who's struggling. A cause you care about. A tired colleague. A family member who's lonely. Now, instead of thinking about everything that would be needed, look at what you actually have. Maybe ten minutes. A skill. A spare meal. A kind word. Five loaves and two fish. Just notice it. Then picture handing it over. If you pray, you can give thanks for it first, the way he did. The bell holds the time.
A boy's lunch. Five barley loaves and two small fish, handed over on a hillside, and five thousand fed with twelve baskets to spare.
Your line: it was enough. Today, offer what you have, even if it's small, before you decide it doesn't count. Day fifty-four.

howItsDone: Many churches read the feeding of the five thousand alongside teaching about communion and about sharing with people in need. Food banks, soup kitchens and church meals often take their inspiration from this story.

original.note: Greek: broken pieces, fragments. What was gathered up so that nothing would be lost.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle about a lot of bread.
what it means: a child hands over a small lunch, it's given thanks for and given away, and it turns out to be enough.
what a scholar hears: barley loaves were poor people's bread, and the words took, gave thanks, gave echo the Last Supper, which is why many Christians hear communion in this meal.

notes: Denarius as a day's wage (Matthew 20:2); two hundred denarii as 'more than half a year's pay'. Confirm.
'The only miracle, apart from the resurrection, told in all four Gospels' — commonly stated; confirm.
Barley as the cheaper grain, bread of the poor; commonly stated; confirm.
'About five thousand men' (John 6:10); the script does not estimate women and children.

The Eucharistic echo (took, gave thanks, distributed; John 6:11 uses eucharistesas) is presented as how many Christians hear it, not as the only reading. The script does not mention the modern 'sharing' reading of the miracle.
